bull.argument: NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 results show exceptional scale. Revenue reached $215.9 billion, up 65%, and operating income rose 60% to $130.4 billion. Data Center revenue grew 68%, driven by the platform shifts to accelerated computing and AI, and management describes the company as now a data center scale AI infrastructure company. Blackwell architectures represented the majority of Data Center revenue, and the company is moving to a one-year product cadence including the Rubin platform. Even amid the $4.5 billion H20 charge, net income grew 65% to $120.1 billion, showing the core franchise absorbed a major shock. Management is also investing to extend its moat: expanding its supply chain into the U.S. and Latin America to add resiliency, and building an AI ecosystem. The risks are real, including supply constraints, export licensing, and customer financing needs, but the filing shows a company with enormous demand momentum and the earnings power to fund its roadmap.

claims.quote: Revenue for fiscal year 2026 was $215.9 billion, up 65% from a year ago. Data Center revenue for fiscal year 2026 was up 68% from a year ago.

bear.argument: The bull case rests on growth, but the filing shows how fragile that growth is. Revenue rose 65%, yet gross margin fell from 75.0% to 71.1%, and management attributes part of the decline to a $4.5 billion H20 charge and to the shift to full-scale Blackwell datacenter solutions. The company also says its ability to meet demand depends on customers' access to data centers, energy, and capital, and notes that access to capital is 'particularly constrained for less-capitalized companies.' Its customers are the ones building the infrastructure, so this is a direct dependency. Meanwhile, NVIDIA is itself financing that ecosystem: it invested $17.5 billion in private companies and provided $3.5 billion in land, power, and shell guarantees to early-stage companies, with the possibility of assuming leases if partners default. Those investments are often illiquid, and the filing offers no assurance of returns. Export licensing adds more uncertainty: H200 licenses have produced no revenue so far, and shipments face a 25% tariff. Earnings strength today does not remove these exposures.

bull.argument: The bear case is fair on risk, but it understates what the filing shows. Gross margin fell 3.9 points, yet gross profit still scaled dramatically on revenue up 65%, and operating income rose 60% to $130.4 billion. The margin decline is explained in the filing by the shift to full-scale Blackwell datacenter solutions and the $4.5 billion H20 charge, which is a one-time, identifiable item rather than evidence of eroding franchise economics. On customer financing, the filing does flag that access to capital is constrained for less-capitalized companies, but it also says the company is now a data center scale AI infrastructure company with Blackwell as the majority of Data Center revenue. The $17.5 billion in investments and $3.5 billion in guarantees are real exposures, and the filing says so plainly. Yet these commitments are also how NVIDIA secures demand in an ecosystem where its own customers need capital, and the company is funding that from earnings. On export, the H200 licensing has produced no revenue to date, and the filing presents that as unknown, not as a settled loss. The fair conclusion is that risks are significant, but the earnings base is large enough to absorb them, and the filing documents a business still growing at scale.

claims.claim: The gross margin decline is attributed in the filing to the shift to Blackwell full-scale datacenter solutions and the H20 charge.
claims.quote: Gross margin decreased in fiscal year 2026 as our business model transitioned from offering Hopper HGX systems to Blackwell full-scale datacenter solutions.

claims.claim: Net income still grew 65% to $120.1 billion despite the margin decline.
Blackwell represented the majority of Data Center revenue, and the company is moving to a one-year product cadence.
claims.quote: Our Blackwell architectures represented the majority of our Data Center revenue.

bear.argument: The bull's answer is that the $4.5 billion H20 charge is a one-time item, but the filing shows margin pressure that is not confined to that charge. Gross margin fell 3.9 points to 71.1%, and the filing attributes part of that to the shift to full-scale Blackwell datacenter solutions, which management says has 'and may in the future cause delays in production,' 'quality issues,' and 'increased inventory provisions.' Those are ongoing transition costs, not a single event. Inventory provisions alone cost 2.6 points of gross margin in fiscal 2026, up from 2.3 points in 2025. Operating income growth also has to be read against operating expenses up 41%. On financing, the bull says the earnings base can absorb commitments, but the filing says the $17.5 billion investments are 'illiquid and non-marketable' and that startups 'may not become profitable... or at all.' The $3.5 billion in guarantees could require NVIDIA to assume leases. Earnings fund these exposures only until the buildout slows, and the filing says customer demand depends on capital that may be scarce. Strong results do not remove that dependency.

claims.claim: Management links the margin decline to ongoing product transition complexity, not only to the H20 charge.
claims.quote: The complexity of our product transitions and sophisticated system configurations has and may in the future cause delays in production and create challenges in managing supply and demand.

claims.claim: Inventory provisions cut gross margin by 2.6 points in fiscal 2026, up from 2.3 points the prior year.
claims.quote: The net effect on our gross margin from inventory provisions and sales of items previously written down was an unfavorable impact of 2.6% in fiscal year 2026 and 2.3% in fiscal year 2025.

claims.claim: Many strategic investments are illiquid and may never return capital.
claims.quote: Many of these investments are illiquid and non‑marketable. The related early-stage startups may not become profitable in the near term, or at all

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes accurately, with the bear's inventory-provision and product-transition quotes directly undercutting the bull's one-time-charge framing. The bull responds fairly to the financing and export risks and keeps the strong earnings base as a counterweight, while the bear rebuts the one-time argument but leans on the 'may not become profitable' language and doesn't fully address why the earnings base cannot absorb the exposures. Overall the debate is evenly matched.
